summary: Clarifies terms and concepts from RFC 3095, the Robust Header Compression framework. It explains ROHC instances, channels, feedback and contexts, and how they relate to network elements and IP interfaces. It updates RFC 3095 and is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Packet labels are long and repeat a lot. ROHC shortens them. This note explains the confusing words people use when talking about it.

subtitle: A glossary and set of pictures that pin down what ROHC instances, channels, feedback and contexts actually are.

tldr.problem: RFC 3095 defines Robust Header Compression (ROHC) but introduces concepts that are hard to understand and hard to relate to the network around them, such as network elements and IP interfaces.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines a precise vocabulary (ROHC instance, ROHC channel, ROHC feedback channel, context) and walks through link examples and figures that show how each piece connects to the others.
tldr.outcome: It is informational and updates RFC 3095. One explicit goal was to support and simplify the ROHC MIB development work.

today: RFC 3759 is an Informational RFC that updates RFC 3095, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why This Document Exists
sections.content:
RFC 3095 defines the RObust Header Compression (ROHC) framework together with 4 compression profiles. The RFC says that many of its concepts are not very extensively defined and described, which can be an obstacle to understanding the standard, especially when thinking about how ROHC relates to the surrounding environments where header compression may be used.

The purpose is to clarify these aspects through examples and additional terminology. It covers ROHC instances, channels, feedback and contexts, and relates them to terms such as network elements and IP interfaces, which are commonly used when addressing MIB issues. One explicit goal is to support and simplify the ROHC MIB development work.
sections.plainLanguage: The first ROHC paper used a lot of words that were easy to mix up. This paper explains them with pictures.

sections.title: Core Terms and Link Examples
sections.content:
The RFC prefers the term network element over "nodes" or "network devices", because network management favors it. A network element talks through one or several IP interfaces, and each IP interface hides the link technology below it. Below an interface sit one or more logical channels, which can be bi-directional or unidirectional.

The two questions that matter for header compression are whether channels are bi- or unidirectional, and whether the link is point-to-point. If it is not, a lower layer addressing scheme is needed to create logical point-to-point channels.

Four example links are given:

  • A satellite link with one unidirectional channel. With no return path, only unidirectional header compression can be applied.
  • A PPP modem connection over a telephone line, with one bi-directional channel. The compression scheme can use the return path to improve performance.
  • An Ethernet, a bi-directional multipoint link with a shared channel. Compression would need a lower layer addressing scheme to give logical point-to-point channels.
  • A cellular wireless link with several channels (the example has one bi-directional and one unidirectional in each direction), where compression applies per channel.

Bi-directional compression means the decompressor can send feedback to the compressor to improve performance. Unidirectional compression means there is no such means.
sections.plainLanguage: A link is like a road between two towns. Some roads are one-way (a satellite), some are two-way (a phone line), and some have many lanes (a cell phone link). Which kind you have decides how smart the shrinking can be.

sections.title: ROHC Instances and ROHC Channels
sections.content:
A ROHC instance is a logical entity that does header compression or decompression using one or several ROHC profiles. It is either a compressor instance or a decompressor instance, never both: when both are present at one place, they count as two instances. An IP interface can have N compressors and M decompressors, where N and M are arbitrary.

A ROHC channel is always unidirectional. It has one input end, connected to the compressed output (CO) of one compressor, and one output end, connected to the compressed input (CI) of one decompressor. Those two are called ROHC peers. Over a bi-directional lower-layer channel, a common case is to allocate one ROHC channel in each direction.

A compressor has 3 inputs and 1 output, and a decompressor has 1 input and 3 outputs, as the figure lists. The RFC notes that its figures in sections 4 to 6 are rotated 90 degrees and do not show a stack view.
sections.plainLanguage: Each shrinker has its own one-way tube to exactly one unshrinker. A shrinker and an unshrinker standing side by side still count as two separate helpers.

sections.title: Feedback Channels
sections.content:
Since ROHC channels always run from compressor to decompressor, a separate concept is needed for the way back. A ROHC feedback channel is a logically dedicated unidirectional channel from a decompressor (its feedback output, FO) to its peer compressor (its feedback input, FI). It must be available and dedicated to the ROHC peers if bi-directional compression is to be allowed. The RFC says there are no other restrictions on how to realize it.

Three non-exhaustive examples are given:

  • Single-channel dedicated: one bi-directional channel carries a ROHC channel one way and a dedicated feedback channel the other way. Piggybacking and interspersing are not used. Two-way compression needs an identical setup in the other direction, giving four logical unidirectional channels.
  • Piggybacked or interspersed: a bi-directional channel carries one ROHC channel in each direction, and feedback rides inside the compressed packets going the other way. Feedback sent as stand-alone packets is interspersed; feedback encapsulated within compressed packets is piggybacked. This needs co-located compressor/decompressor pairs that are associated with each other.
  • Dual-channel dedicated: two bi-directional channels carry two ROHC channels and two dedicated feedback channels.
sections.plainLanguage: Feedback is a return note from the unshrinker saying how things are going. It can have its own tube, or it can hitch a ride on the tube going the other way.

sections.title: Contexts and Context Identifiers
sections.content:
Each compressor or decompressor can handle an arbitrary but limited number of concurrent packet streams over its ROHC channel. Each stream relates to one context. Compressed packets carry a context identifier (CID) saying which context they belong to, so there is a one-to-one mapping between the contexts and the CID space used on that ROHC channel.

Each ROHC instance at an IP interface has its own context and CID space. The RFC requires care that the CID size of the corresponding decompressor is not smaller than the CID space of the compressor.

Section 8 sums up the relationships: a network element has one or several IP interfaces, each connected to one or several logical layer two channels; each interface may have several ROHC instances; each instance has exactly one ROHC channel and optionally exactly one feedback channel. There is no general relation between ROHC instances and layer two channels, since that depends on how channels are realized.
sections.plainLanguage: If many conversations share one tube, each note is stamped with a number saying which conversation it belongs to. The number lets the other side keep the notes sorted.

sections.title: Implementation and Security Notes
sections.content:
ROHC is a general framework on top of which profiles are defined. The split between framework and profiles is mainly a standardization split, so implementing the framework as a separate module is not an obvious choice, especially if profile implementations come from different vendors. Optimized implementations will probably separate the common parts into a framework module and add profile modules. If vendor and version information is exposed for network management, the RFC says it should be per profile, and potentially for the instance as a whole.

On security, the RFC says that a clear understanding of ROHC channels and their relation to IP interfaces and the physical medium plays a critical role in secure usage. It is a useful addition to the Security Considerations of RFC 3095, but since it only reviews information and definitions, it adds no new security issues.
sections.plainLanguage: When people build ROHC, they might put the shared parts in one box and each shrinking recipe in its own box. Because this paper only gives names to things, it does not add any new dangers.

viz.caption: THE 8 CONNECTION POINTS OF COMPRESSOR AND DECOMPRESSOR

items.label: Uncompressed Input
items.desc: Compressor input: uncompressed packets from higher layers.

items.label: Compressed Output
items.desc: Compressor output: always connected to the input end of a ROHC channel.

items.label: Feedback Input
items.desc: Compressor input, optional: feedback from the corresponding decompressor.

items.label: Piggyback Input
items.desc: Compressor input, optional: feedback to piggyback for a co-located decompressor.

items.label: Compressed Input
items.desc: Decompressor input: always connected to the output end of a ROHC channel.

items.label: Decompressed Output
items.desc: Decompressor output: decompressed packets for higher layers.

items.label: Feedback Output
items.desc: Decompressor output, optional: feedback to the corresponding compressor.

items.label: Piggyback Output
items.desc: Decompressor output, optional: received piggybacked feedback for a co-located compressor.
